question_text: Q1. Micro-organisms responsible for hospital-acquired pneumonia are:
options: a) Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila
b) Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, parainfluenza virus
c) Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae
d) Pneumocystis carinii, cytomegalovirus, Aspergillus fumigatus
answer: Answer: C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae
rationale: Rationale: Hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia is typically caused by virulent, often resistant Gram-negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus - e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae and S. aureus. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Mycoplasma cause community-acquired pneumonia, while Pneumocystis/CMV/Aspergillus affect the immunocompromised. (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth.)

question_text: Q2. Bioavailability of drugs taken by mouth is affected by:
options: a) Water-solubility, blood flow through the kidneys, normal liver function
b) Capacity of liver enzymes to metabolise, age of the patient, extent of protein binding
c) Distribution volume, weight of the patient, ability of drug to cross membranes
d) Acidity of the stomach, transit time through the digestive tract, presence of food
answer: Answer: D) Acidity of the stomach, transit time through the digestive tract, presence of food
rationale: Rationale: Oral bioavailability is the fraction of an oral dose reaching the systemic circulation; it depends mainly on absorption from the gut, which is influenced by gastric acidity (pH), gastrointestinal transit time/motility and the presence of food. (First-pass metabolism also contributes, but the option that directly describes oral absorption factors is D.) (Ref: Pharmacology - pharmacokinetics.)

question_text: Q3. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is:
options: a) Responsible for secondary antibody response
b) Produced when an antigen is encountered for the first time
c) Responsible for defence against invasion of micro-organisms through the body's mucous membranes
d) The mediator of immediate reactions
answer: Answer: A) Responsible for secondary antibody response
rationale: Rationale: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin and the principal antibody of the SECONDARY (memory) immune response; it also crosses the placenta to confer passive immunity. IgM is produced on first antigen exposure, IgA protects mucous membranes/secretions, and IgE mediates immediate (allergic) reactions. (Ref: Microbiology/Immunology - Kenyan curriculum.)

question_text: Q4. The cell-mediated immune system is made up of:
answer: Answer: A) T-lymphocytes and macrophages
rationale: Rationale: Cell-mediated immunity is effected by T-lymphocytes together with phagocytic cells such as macrophages (which present antigen and are activated by T cells). Antibodies and B-lymphocytes belong to humoral immunity. (Ref: Microbiology/Immunology - Kenyan curriculum.)

question_text: Q1. The drugs that are classified as cephalosporins include:
answer: Answer: A) Cefixime, Loracarbef
rationale: Rationale: Cephalosporins are a class of beta-lactam antibiotics; cefixime and loracarbef both belong to this class. The other options pair a cephalosporin with a non-antibiotic - Laroxyl (amitriptyline), Lasix (furosemide) and clonazepam (a benzodiazepine). (Ref: Pharmacology - antimicrobials.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q2. The antitussive agents are indicated for:
options: a) Removing excess mucus from the airway
answer: Answer: D) Relieving a dry (non-productive) cough
rationale: Rationale: Antitussives (e.g. codeine, dextromethorphan) suppress the cough reflex and are indicated for a dry, irritating, non-productive cough. They are NOT used for a productive cough (which should be retained to clear secretions). (Ref: Pharmacology - respiratory drugs.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q3. The nurse should instruct a client who is taking an expectorant to:
answer: Answer: B) Increase fluid intake
rationale: Rationale: Expectorants (e.g. guaifenesin) increase respiratory tract fluid to liquefy and loosen secretions; the client should increase fluid intake (and humidify the air) to enhance their effect. Antihistamines dry secretions and are counterproductive. (Ref: Pharmacology - respiratory drugs.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q4. The drugs that are classified as narcotic analgesics include:
answer: Answer: C) Codeine, Morphine
rationale: Rationale: Narcotic (opioid) analgesics act on opioid receptors in the CNS - codeine and morphine are both opioids. The other options contain NSAIDs/non-opioids (aspirin, indomethacin, ibuprofen, diclofenac) or mixtures of an opioid with an NSAID. (Ref: Pharmacology - analgesics.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q5. The action of hypnotic drugs is to induce:
answer: Answer: C) Sleep
rationale: Rationale: Hypnotic drugs (e.g. benzodiazepines, zolpidem) act on the CNS to induce and maintain sleep. (Sedatives calm/reduce anxiety; in higher dose hypnotics produce sleep.) (Ref: Pharmacology - CNS depressants.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q6. The antidote for morphine toxicity is:
answer: Answer: D) Naloxone
rationale: Rationale: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist and the specific antidote for morphine (opioid) overdose, rapidly reversing respiratory depression. Methadone and fentanyl are themselves opioids. (Ref: Pharmacology; MOH Kenya emergency management of poisoning.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q7. The extent to which a drug is absorbed and transported to the target tissue is known as:
answer: Answer: C) Bioavailability
rationale: Rationale: Bioavailability is the fraction (extent) of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation (and thus the target tissue) in active form. Half-life is the time for the plasma concentration to fall by half. (Ref: Pharmacology - pharmacokinetics.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q8. The actions of the body on the drug are referred to as:
answer: Answer: B) Pharmacokinetics
rationale: Rationale: Pharmacokinetics is what the BODY does to the drug - absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). Pharmacodynamics is what the DRUG does to the body. (Ref: Pharmacology - basic principles.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q9. Atenolol is a/an:
answer: Answer: B) Beta-blocker
rationale: Rationale: Atenolol is a cardioselective beta-adrenergic blocker (beta-blocker) used in hypertension, angina and after myocardial infarction; it lowers heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand. (Ref: Pharmacology - cardiovascular drugs.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q10. The drugs that are classified as penicillins include:
answer: Answer: A) Methicillin sodium, Nafcillin sodium
rationale: Rationale: Methicillin and nafcillin are both penicillinase-resistant penicillins. The other options pair a penicillin with a non-penicillin - ciprofloxacin (a quinolone), doxycycline (a tetracycline), erythromycin (a macrolide) and sotalol (a beta-blocker). (Ref: Pharmacology - antimicrobials.)
source: [Source paper: September 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q11. An example of a drug derived from a plant is:
answer: Answer: B) Quinine
rationale: Rationale: Quinine is an alkaloid obtained from the bark of the cinchona plant - a classic plant-derived (botanical) drug used in malaria. (Ref: Pharmacology - sources of drugs.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q12. The route of drug administration with the highest drug bioavailability is:
answer: Answer: D) Intravenous
rationale: Rationale: The intravenous route delivers the drug directly into the bloodstream, giving 100% bioavailability (no absorption barrier and no first-pass metabolism). (Ref: Pharmacology - pharmacokinetics.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q13. The following is an opioid antagonist:
answer: Answer: B) Naltrexone
rationale: Rationale: Naltrexone (like naloxone) is an opioid antagonist used in the management of opioid (and alcohol) dependence. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist; sufentanil and methadone are opioid agonists. (Ref: Pharmacology - opioids and antagonists.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q14. The drug used for organophosphate poisoning is:
answer: Answer: A) Atropine
rationale: Rationale: Atropine (an antimuscarinic) is the antidote for organophosphate (anticholinesterase) poisoning; it reverses the muscarinic effects of acetylcholine excess (usually together with pralidoxime). (Ref: Pharmacology; MOH Kenya management of poisoning.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q15. Local anaesthetics work by:
options: a) Blocking calcium ion channels to prevent depolarization
b) Blocking potassium ion channels to prevent depolarization
c) Blocking sodium ion channels to prevent depolarization
d) Blocking impulse at the neuromuscular junction
answer: Answer: C) Blocking sodium ion channels to prevent depolarization
rationale: Rationale: Local anaesthetics (e.g. lignocaine) block voltage-gated SODIUM channels in the nerve membrane, preventing depolarisation and thus the generation and conduction of the nerve impulse. (Ref: Pharmacology - local anaesthetics.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q16. Pregnant women should be advised not to take tetracycline because it has been associated with:
options: b) Tooth and bone defects in the neonate
answer: Answer: B) Tooth and bone defects in the neonate
rationale: Rationale: Tetracyclines are deposited in developing teeth and bones, causing permanent tooth discoloration and impaired bone growth in the foetus/child; they are therefore contraindicated in pregnancy and in young children. (Gray baby syndrome is caused by chloramphenicol.) (Ref: Pharmacology - drugs in pregnancy.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q17. Acyclovir is a drug of choice for treatment of herpes virus. Its mode of action is to:
answer: Answer: B) Inhibit viral DNA synthesis
rationale: Rationale: Acyclovir is phosphorylated within infected cells and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase, thereby blocking viral DNA synthesis/replication. (Ref: Pharmacology - antivirals.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q18. A drug that prevents the release of histamine from mast cells is:
answer: Answer: A) Cromolyn
rationale: Rationale: Cromolyn (sodium cromoglicate) is a mast-cell stabiliser that prevents the release of histamine and other mediators. Cetirizine is an H1-antihistamine (blocks the receptor), aminophylline is a bronchodilator, and montelukast is a leukotriene-receptor antagonist. (Ref: Pharmacology - anti-allergic drugs.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q19. Oral antidiabetics that work by stimulating beta cells to secrete more insulin and increasing receptor sites in the tissues are classified as:
answer: Answer: C) Sulfonylureas
rationale: Rationale: Sulfonylureas (e.g. glibenclamide, gliclazide) lower blood glucose mainly by stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells (and increasing tissue insulin sensitivity). Biguanides (metformin) act mainly by reducing hepatic glucose output. (Ref: Pharmacology - oral hypoglycaemics.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q20. The extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotic drugs include:
answer: Answer: B) Parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, opisthotonus
rationale: Rationale: Extrapyramidal side effects of antipsychotics include drug-induced parkinsonism, acute dystonias (e.g. opisthotonus), akathisia and tardive dyskinesia. Hallucinations are symptoms of the illness, not an extrapyramidal drug effect. (Ref: Pharmacology - antipsychotics.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q21. Combined chemotherapy of tuberculosis is used to:
options: d) Decrease the onset of antimycobacterial drug biotransformation
answer: Answer: A) Decrease mycobacterial drug resistance
rationale: Rationale: Tuberculosis is treated with a combination of drugs to prevent (decrease) the emergence of drug-resistant mycobacteria, since resistance readily develops when a single drug is used. (Ref: MOH Kenya National TB programme; Pharmacology.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q22. When teaching about the proper use of antacids, a nurse should instruct the client to:
options: a) Stagger the administration of antacids with other medications
b) Take the antacids with all other medications
c) Take other medications in the daytime and antacids at night
d) Drink a glass of water immediately after taking the antacids
answer: Answer: A) Stagger the administration of antacids with other medications
rationale: Rationale: Antacids alter gastric pH and bind many drugs, reducing their absorption; the client should therefore stagger (separate by 1-2 hours) antacid intake from other oral medications. (Ref: Pharmacology - GIT drugs/drug interactions.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q23. A 9-year-old schoolgirl has been diagnosed with taeniasis. The drug of choice in this case would be:
answer: Answer: B) Praziquantel
rationale: Rationale: Taeniasis (tapeworm infestation) is treated with praziquantel, the drug of choice. Diethylcarbamazine is used for filariasis and ivermectin for onchocerciasis/strongyloidiasis. (Ref: Pharmacology - anthelmintics; MOH Kenya.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q24. 4-aminoquinoline derivative antimalarial drugs include:
answer: Answer: C) Amodiaquine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine
rationale: Rationale: The 4-aminoquinolines are chloroquine, amodiaquine and hydroxychloroquine. Quinine is a quinoline-methanol; mefloquine is a 4-quinoline-methanol; artesunate/artemether are artemisinin derivatives. (Ref: Pharmacology - antimalarials.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q25. The drugs that are classified as diuretics include:
answer: Answer: A) Mannitol, Acetazolamide
rationale: Rationale: Mannitol (an osmotic diuretic) and acetazolamide (a carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor diuretic) are both diuretics. The distractors pair a diuretic with a non-diuretic - digoxin (cardiac glycoside), theophylline (bronchodilator) and amytal (a barbiturate). (Ref: Pharmacology - diuretics.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q26. The drug used to treat methotrexate toxicity is:
answer: Answer: B) Folinic acid
rationale: Rationale: Folinic acid (leucovorin/calcium folinate) is the 'rescue' antidote for methotrexate toxicity; it supplies reduced folate, bypassing the dihydrofolate-reductase block produced by methotrexate. (Ref: Pharmacology - antineoplastics/antidotes.)
source: [Source paper: June 2018 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper III]

question_text: Q1. The major contraindication of Praziquantel is its use in patients with:
answer: Answer: B) Ocular cysticercosis
rationale: Rationale: Praziquantel is contraindicated in ocular cysticercosis because killing the parasite within the eye provokes an inflammatory reaction that can cause irreversible ocular damage. (Ref: Pharmacology - anthelmintics; WHO.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q2. The major side effects of Indomethacin on the cardiovascular system are:
answer: Answer: D) Hypertension, oedema
rationale: Rationale: Indomethacin is an NSAID; by inhibiting prostaglandins it causes sodium and water retention, leading to oedema and raised blood pressure (hypertension). (Ref: Pharmacology - NSAIDs.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q3. The time that is required to reduce the concentration of a drug in the body by one half is called:
answer: Answer: C) Half-life
rationale: Rationale: The half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for the plasma concentration (or amount) of a drug in the body to fall by one half; it guides dosing frequency. (Ref: Pharmacology - pharmacokinetics.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q4. The drugs that are classified as sulphonamides include:
answer: Answer: A) Cotrimoxazole, Sulfamethoxazole, Sulfasalazine
rationale: Rationale: Sulphonamides include sulfamethoxazole (a component of cotrimoxazole) and sulfasalazine. The distractors include non-sulphonamides such as spironolactone (a diuretic), sulfinpyrazone (a uricosuric) and cefpodoxime (a cephalosporin). (Ref: Pharmacology - antimicrobials.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q5. The drugs that have almost exclusively harmful effects in the body are known as:
answer: Answer: D) Poisons
rationale: Rationale: Poisons are substances whose effects on the body are essentially harmful. (Elixirs are sweetened hydro-alcoholic drug solutions; xenobiotics are any substances foreign to the body, not necessarily harmful.) (Ref: Pharmacology/Toxicology - basic concepts.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q6. The possibility of harmful effects on the foetus during the formative stages of development is referred to as:
answer: Answer: B) Teratogenicity
rationale: Rationale: Teratogenicity is the capacity of an agent (drug, chemical, infection, radiation) to cause structural or functional abnormalities in the developing embryo/foetus. (Ref: Pharmacology - drugs in pregnancy.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q7. The mode of action of Nifedipine (Adalat) is that it:
options: a) Inhibits calcium ion influx across cardiac and smooth muscle cells, decreasing myocardial contractility and oxygen demand
b) Stabilizes the neuronal membrane and limits seizure activity
c) Depresses monosynaptic and polysynaptic transmission in the CNS
d) Increases the amount of noradrenaline or serotonin in the central nervous system
answer: Answer: A) Inhibits calcium ion influx across cardiac and smooth muscle cells, decreasing myocardial contractility and oxygen demand
rationale: Rationale: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker: it inhibits calcium ion influx into cardiac and vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilatation and reducing myocardial contractility and oxygen demand (used in hypertension and angina). (Ref: Pharmacology - cardiovascular drugs.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q8. Diclofenac sodium produces anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic effects possibly by inhibiting the synthesis of:
answer: Answer: B) Prostaglandin
rationale: Rationale: Diclofenac is an NSAID that inhibits cyclo-oxygenase, thereby blocking PROSTAGLANDIN synthesis - producing anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic effects. (Ref: Pharmacology - NSAIDs.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q9. The antiulcer agents include:
answer: Answer: C) Famotidine, Sucralfate
rationale: Rationale: Famotidine (an H2-receptor antagonist) and sucralfate (a mucosal protective agent) are both anti-ulcer drugs. The distractors pair an anti-ulcer drug with an unrelated agent - Laroxyl (amitriptyline), tramadol (an analgesic) and praziquantel (an anthelmintic). (Ref: Pharmacology - drugs for peptic ulcer disease.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q10. The mode of action of salbutamol sulphate is that it:
options: a) Inhibits phosphodiesterase, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle and pulmonary blood vessels
b) Relaxes bronchial and uterine smooth muscle by acting on beta-adrenergic receptors
c) Stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors within the sympathetic nervous system
d) Inhibits vagally mediated reflexes by antagonising acetylcholine
answer: Answer: B) Relaxes bronchial and uterine smooth muscle by acting on beta-adrenergic receptors
rationale: Rationale: Salbutamol is a selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist; stimulating beta-2 receptors relaxes bronchial smooth muscle (bronchodilation) and uterine smooth muscle (tocolysis). (Ref: Pharmacology - respiratory drugs.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q11. The anti-anxiety agents include:
answer: Answer: C) Meprobamate, Chlordiazepoxide
rationale: Rationale: Meprobamate and chlordiazepoxide are both anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) agents. The distractors include aminophylline (a bronchodilator), ranitidine (an anti-ulcer drug) and simethicone (an anti-flatulent). (Ref: Pharmacology - anxiolytics.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q12. The component of a cell or organism that interacts with a drug and initiates the chain of events leading to the drug's observed effects is called:
answer: Answer: D) A receptor
rationale: Rationale: A receptor is the cellular macromolecule with which a drug interacts to initiate its effects. An agonist is a drug that activates a receptor; an antagonist blocks it. (Ref: Pharmacology - pharmacodynamics.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q13. The mode of action of gentamicin sulphate is:
options: a) Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
d) Inhibition of folic acid (DHF reductase)
answer: Answer: B) Inhibition of protein synthesis
rationale: Rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside; it binds the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis. (Beta-lactams inhibit cell-wall synthesis; quinolones inhibit DNA synthesis; sulphonamides/trimethoprim inhibit folate synthesis.) (Ref: Pharmacology - antimicrobials.)
source: [Source paper: May 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q14. The effect of combining drugs, where one drug which has no effect increases the effects of another drug, is termed:
answer: Answer: A) Potentiation
rationale: Rationale: Potentiation occurs when a drug that has little or no effect of its own increases (enhances) the effect of another drug. Antagonism is opposition of effects; additive/summation is when two active drugs' effects add up. (Ref: Pharmacology - drug interactions.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q15. Ipratropium bromide is:
options: a) A cholinergic agent used for perennial rhinitis
b) An anticholinergic used for allergic rhinitis and colds
c) Only used in patients with asthma
d) Inappropriate for use in allergic rhinitis
answer: Answer: B) An anticholinergic used for allergic rhinitis and colds
rationale: Rationale: Ipratropium bromide is an ANTICHOLINERGIC (antimuscarinic). As an inhaled bronchodilator it is used in asthma and COPD, and as a nasal spray it dries secretions in allergic/non-allergic rhinitis and the common cold - so it is not 'cholinergic' nor limited to asthma. (Ref: Pharmacology - respiratory/autonomic drugs.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q16. The route of drug administration with the highest compliance from patients is:
answer: Answer: C) Oral
rationale: Rationale: The oral route gives the highest patient compliance because it is convenient, non-invasive, painless and can be self-administered. (The intravenous route gives the highest bioavailability but poorer compliance.) (Ref: Pharmacology - routes of administration.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q17. A patient on anti-ulcer therapy complains of reduced libido and impotence. The nurse informs him that it may be associated with:
answer: Answer: B) Cimetidine
rationale: Rationale: Cimetidine has anti-androgenic effects and can cause gynaecomastia, reduced libido and impotence in men (and is also a potent enzyme inhibitor). The other H2-blockers rarely do so. (Ref: Pharmacology - drugs for peptic ulcer disease.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q18. Bulk-forming laxatives:
options: d) Are used to prepare the bowel for diagnostic procedures
answer: Answer: A) Function like dietary fibre
rationale: Rationale: Bulk-forming laxatives (e.g. psyllium/methylcellulose) act like dietary fibre - they absorb water and swell to increase faecal bulk, stimulating peristalsis. They act slowly (1-3 days), not in 2-6 hours, and are not used for bowel preparation (that requires stimulant/osmotic agents). (Ref: Pharmacology - GIT drugs.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q19. Diazepam exerts its effects by:
options: a) Binding on GABA receptors in the brain
c) Blocking acetylcholine at the synaptic cleft
d) Increasing the influx of sodium into neurons
answer: Answer: A) Binding on GABA receptors in the brain
rationale: Rationale: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine; it binds the GABA-A receptor complex and enhances the inhibitory action of GABA (increasing chloride influx), producing anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects. (Ref: Pharmacology - CNS depressants.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q20. In a patient suffering from angina, nitroglycerin may be given sublingually because this mode of administration:
options: b) Causes less reflex tachycardia than oral administration
answer: Answer: D) Avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism
rationale: Rationale: Sublingual nitroglycerin is absorbed directly into the systemic circulation through the oral mucosa, AVOIDING first-pass hepatic metabolism (which would otherwise inactivate most of the drug), giving rapid relief of angina. (Ref: Pharmacology - antianginal drugs.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q21. The most appropriate drug for treatment of bacillary dysentery in adults is:
answer: Answer: A) Ciprofloxacin
rationale: Rationale: Bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) in adults is treated with ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), the recommended first-line agent owing to widespread resistance to older drugs. (Ref: MOH Kenya/WHO management of dysentery.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q22. The commonest side effect associated with morphine is:
answer: Answer: C) Constipation
rationale: Rationale: Constipation is the most common and persistent adverse effect of morphine (and other opioids), because opioids reduce gastrointestinal motility; unlike other opioid effects, tolerance to constipation does not develop, so a laxative is usually prescribed. (Ref: Pharmacology - opioid analgesics.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q23. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in HIV infection is associated with:
options: a) An increase in the rate of emergence of drug resistance
b) A decrease in CD4 count
c) A decrease in viral RNA in the blood
d) An increased incidence of opportunistic infections
answer: Answer: C) A decrease in viral RNA in the blood
rationale: Rationale: Effective HAART suppresses viral replication, producing a fall in plasma viral RNA (viral load), a rise in CD4 count and fewer opportunistic infections. Combination therapy is designed to REDUCE (not increase) the emergence of resistance. (Ref: NASCOP/MOH Kenya ARV guidelines.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q24. Beta-lactamase production is a mechanism of resistance among strains of Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Which of the following drugs is effective against the above organisms?
answer: Answer: B) Ceftriaxone
rationale: Rationale: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that is stable to many beta-lactamases and is effective against beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and N. gonorrhoeae. Amoxicillin and ticarcillin are readily hydrolysed by beta-lactamases. (Ref: Pharmacology - antimicrobials; MOH Kenya STI guidelines.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q25. Regarding warfarin:
options: a) It is a rapid-acting anticoagulant
b) It has poor absorption across membranes
c) It has teratogenic effects when administered in pregnancy
d) It is administered through the intravenous route
answer: Answer: C) It has teratogenic effects when administered in pregnancy
rationale: Rationale: Warfarin is teratogenic (causes fetal warfarin syndrome) and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is a SLOW-acting ORAL anticoagulant (heparin is the rapid-acting/parenteral agent) and is well absorbed. (Ref: Pharmacology - anticoagulants.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q26. Cromolyn is useful in asthma because it:
options: a) Suppresses the release of histamine
b) Blocks adenosine receptors in the smooth muscles of bronchioles
d) Decreases bacterial load in the bronchioles
answer: Answer: A) Suppresses the release of histamine
rationale: Rationale: Cromolyn (sodium cromoglicate) is a mast-cell stabiliser; it prevents the release of histamine and other mediators from mast cells, and is used for prophylaxis (not relief) of asthma. (Ref: Pharmacology - anti-asthmatic drugs.)
source: [Source paper: February 2019 - KMTC Pharmacology, KRCHN-B Paper V]

question_text: Q1. The first scientific paper in nursing was published by:
answer: Answer: B) Florence Nightingale
rationale: Rationale: Florence Nightingale is regarded as the founder of modern nursing and the first nurse researcher; through her statistical 'Notes' she produced the first scientific writing in nursing. (Ref: Foundations of Nursing / Nursing research texts.)

question_text: Q2. The graduate nurse's role in research is:
options: a) Intelligent consumption of research findings
answer: Answer: A) Intelligent consumption of research findings
rationale: Rationale: At the generalist/graduate level the expected competency is to be an intelligent CONSUMER of research - critically appraising and applying evidence (evidence-based practice) to care. Designing and leading studies is the role of nurses with advanced (master's/doctoral) preparation. (Ref: Nursing Research - Kenyan curriculum; Polit & Beck.)

question_text: Q3. A nurse researcher formulated the following hypothesis: “There is a relationship between self-concept and suicidal behaviour”. This implies that:
options: a) The independent variable is suicidal behaviour
c) The type of design suggested would be experimental
d) The dependent variable is suicidal behaviour
answer: Answer: D) The dependent variable is suicidal behaviour
rationale: Rationale: Self-concept is the presumed influencing (independent) variable and suicidal behaviour is the outcome (dependent) variable. The statement merely asserts 'a relationship' without specifying its direction, so it is NON-directional, and a relationship hypothesis suggests a correlational (not experimental) design. (Ref: Nursing Research; Polit & Beck.)

question_text: Q4. Theoretical framework refers to:
options: a) A comprehensive list of all the relevant previous research work done in an area of interest
c) A pictorial presentation of relationships between variables
d) An examination of both the depth and breadth of literature review
answer: Answer: B) Roy's adaptation theory
rationale: Rationale: A theoretical framework is the underpinning of a study built on an established, tested theory; Roy's Adaptation Model is a classic example of such a theory used to frame nursing studies. (A) describes a literature review; (C) describes a conceptual framework/model; (D) describes critiquing the literature. (Ref: Nursing Research; Polit & Beck.)

question_text: Q5. Trait leadership theories in nursing:
options: a) Focus on what leaders do in relational and contextual terms
b) Emphasise the degrees of trust and respect between leaders and followers
c) Are independent of personal characteristics of followers
d) Emphasise that physical and emotional characteristics are critical in inspiring others toward a common goal
answer: Answer: D) Emphasise that physical and emotional characteristics are critical in inspiring others toward a common goal
rationale: Rationale: Trait theory holds that leaders possess inborn personal characteristics (physical, emotional, intellectual qualities such as drive, self-confidence and integrity) that make them able to lead and inspire others. Behavioural theories focus on what leaders do (A); transformational/relational theories emphasise trust and respect (B). (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management - Kenyan curriculum.)

question_text: Q6. The main purpose of publishing research findings is to:
options: a) Meet the requirements of the sponsor
b) Solicit for more funds for future research
c) Get recognition in the profession
answer: Answer: D) Contribute to scientific literature
rationale: Rationale: Dissemination through publication adds to the body of scientific/professional knowledge, allowing findings to be utilised and built upon (evidence-based practice). The other options may be secondary benefits but are not the main purpose. (Ref: Nursing Research.)

question_text: Q7. While conducting research among psychiatric patients, the nurse researcher:
options: b) May interview the patients directly if they attain a specified mental health status
c) Must get consent from relatives and guardians only
answer: Answer: B) May interview the patients directly if they attain a specified mental health status
rationale: Rationale: Psychiatric patients are a vulnerable group; the researcher may interview them directly (and obtain their own informed consent) provided their mental state allows them to understand and consent competently. Consent is not limited to relatives/guardians, and the data source is not restricted to key informants. (Ref: Research ethics - Nursing Research.)

question_text: Q8. Discovery learning approach:
options: a) Is more effective than expounding the principles then engaging the students in learning
b) Takes less time than the exposition learning approach
c) Helps students attain higher-level (life-skill) or methodological objectives as opposed to being passive receivers
d) Is best applied when students need to grasp a few basic concepts
answer: Answer: C) Helps students attain higher-level (life-skill) or methodological objectives as opposed to being passive receivers
rationale: Rationale: Discovery (inquiry) learning engages learners actively in finding out for themselves, which is best suited to attaining higher-order/methodological and life-skill objectives rather than producing passive recipients. It typically takes MORE time and is not ideal for transmitting a few simple facts. (Ref: Nursing Education / principles of teaching & learning.)

question_text: Q9. Micro-evaluation:
options: a) Enables the teacher to launch into new lines of argument when the students seem unconvinced
b) Enables students to benefit in some future learning situations
c) Should be minimal and limited if students are working together
answer: Answer: A) Enables the teacher to launch into new lines of argument when the students seem unconvinced
rationale: Rationale: Micro-evaluation is the moment-to-moment, formative feedback a teacher obtains DURING a lesson (e.g. reading the learners' reactions), allowing immediate adjustment of the teaching - such as opening new lines of explanation when students appear unconvinced. (Ref: Nursing Education / evaluation in teaching.)

question_text: Q1. A leader who is mainly concerned with the day-to-day operations of an organisation with little regard to the future is called a:
answer: Answer: B) Transactional leader
rationale: Rationale: A transactional leader focuses on day-to-day operations, supervision, exchange (rewards/penalties) and maintaining the status quo, rather than on vision and future transformation (the focus of a transformational leader). (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management.)

question_text: Q2. Zero-based budgeting means:
options: a) Multiplying current year expenses by a certain figure
b) Budgeting for purchase of major equipment
c) Use of a decision-making package to justify the current budget needs
d) Budget where accountability, efficiency and economy is emphasized
answer: Answer: C) Use of a decision-making package to justify the current budget needs
rationale: Rationale: In zero-based budgeting every programme/activity starts from a 'zero base' and each manager must justify all requested funds afresh each period using decision packages - nothing is automatically carried over from the previous budget. (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management - budgeting.)

question_text: Q3. Mentors differ from preceptors in that mentors:
options: c) Have a short relationship with the novice staff
d) Do not assist the novice staff in career development
answer: Answer: B) Choose whom to mentor
rationale: Rationale: Mentoring is a voluntary, mutually chosen and usually long-term developmental relationship - the mentor chooses (and is chosen by) the protege and actively supports career development. A preceptor is normally assigned for a defined, shorter orientation period. (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management / Education.)

question_text: Q4. Over-delegation involves:
options: a) Delegating at the wrong time, to the wrong person, for the wrong reasons
b) Delegating to exceptionally competent employees
c) Transferring too many roles from the manager to the subordinates
answer: Answer: C) Transferring too many roles from the manager to the subordinates
rationale: Rationale: Over-delegation is delegating TOO MUCH - transferring excessive tasks/roles (often including those the manager should retain) to subordinates, overloading them. (Improper delegation = wrong task/time/person; under-delegation = delegating too little.) (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management - delegation.)

question_text: Q5. Variables that take only a few discrete values are called:
answer: Answer: D) Categorical
rationale: Rationale: Categorical (discrete) variables take a limited number of distinct values or categories (e.g. sex, blood group), in contrast to continuous variables which can take any value along a range. (Ref: Nursing Research / Biostatistics.)

question_text: Q6. In research journal articles, “blind reviews” means reviewers:
options: a) Are told the names of the researchers and the researchers are not told the identity of the reviewers
b) Are not told the names of the researchers and the researchers are told the identity of the reviewers
c) Are not told the names of the researchers and the researchers are not told the identity of the reviewers
d) Know the names of the researchers and vice versa
answer: Answer: C) Are not told the names of the researchers and the researchers are not told the identity of the reviewers
rationale: Rationale: A (double-) blind review is one in which the reviewers are not told who the authors are AND the authors are not told who the reviewers are - protecting objectivity and reducing bias. (Ref: Nursing Research - publication/peer review.)

question_text: Q7. It is difficult to obtain meaningful informed consent in qualitative research because the researcher does not know in advance how the study will evolve. This kind of consent gotten by qualitative research is called:
answer: Answer: A) Process consent
rationale: Rationale: In qualitative research, because the design unfolds, consent is treated as an ongoing process - 'process consent' - in which the researcher repeatedly renegotiates the participant's continued agreement as the study evolves. (Ref: Nursing Research - qualitative methods/ethics.)

question_text: Q8. Random assignment means:
options: a) Probability sampling where each subject has an equal and independent chance of participating in the study
b) Assigning subjects to the control and experimental group without predetermined criteria
c) Assigning subjects to the control group and experimental group such that each has an equal chance of being selected for each group
d) Random sampling method of assigning subjects to control group and experimental group
answer: Answer: C) Assigning subjects to the control group and experimental group such that each has an equal chance of being selected for each group
rationale: Rationale: Random assignment (randomisation) is the allocation of subjects to study groups so that each participant has an equal and independent chance of being placed in EITHER the control or the experimental group - it controls for confounding. (Random selection/sampling, by contrast, concerns who gets INTO the study.) (Ref: Nursing Research - experimental design.)

question_text: Q9. Practising nurses need to develop research-critique skills to:
options: a) Challenge fellow nurses doing research-report presentations
b) Be able to do literature review when doing their research studies
c) Participate fully in journal clubs
d) Judge the utility of research findings
answer: Answer: D) Judge the utility of research findings
rationale: Rationale: The purpose of developing research-critique (appraisal) skills is to enable nurses to judge the quality and utility of research findings so they can decide whether and how to apply the evidence in practice (evidence-based practice). (Ref: Nursing Research.)

question_text: Q10. Reflective scepticism, a characteristic of critical thinkers, means:
options: a) Asking awkward questions to challenge assumptions
b) Ability to imagine and explore alternatives
c) Taking a critical view of established dogmas and practices, scrutinizing them and questioning their current validity
d) Reflecting on past events and questioning them
answer: Answer: C) Taking a critical view of established dogmas and practices, scrutinizing them and questioning their current validity
rationale: Rationale: Reflective scepticism is the disposition not to accept established dogmas/practices at face value - critically scrutinising them and questioning their current validity and evidence base. (Ref: Nursing Education - critical thinking.)

question_text: Q11. Problem-based learning means:
options: a) Learning that results from the process of working towards the resolution of a problem
b) A situation where students learn without any assistance from the teacher
c) Learning that results after the learner gets the solution
d) Learning where teachers use questions only
answer: Answer: A) Learning that results from the process of working towards the resolution of a problem
rationale: Rationale: Problem-based learning (PBL) is a student-centred approach in which learning arises from the PROCESS of working to understand and resolve a real or simulated problem; the teacher facilitates rather than abandons the learners. (Ref: Nursing Education - teaching/learning methods.)

question_text: Q12. When an assessment tool measures what it is supposed to measure, it is said to have:
answer: Answer: A) Validity
rationale: Rationale: Validity is the degree to which an instrument actually measures what it is intended to measure. Reliability/consistency refers to the stability/reproducibility of the measurement. (Ref: Nursing Research / Educational measurement.)

question_text: Q13. An appropriate method that can be used to teach the acquisition of psychomotor skills is:
answer: Answer: B) Demonstration
rationale: Rationale: Psychomotor (practical) skills are best taught by demonstration (and return demonstration), which shows the learner exactly how to perform the procedure step by step. Case studies and brainstorming target cognitive/affective domains. (Ref: Nursing Education - teaching methods.)

question_text: Q14. The decision-making hierarchy is called:
answer: Answer: A) Scalar chain
rationale: Rationale: The scalar chain is the formal line of authority and communication running from the top to the bottom of an organisation (the chain of command/hierarchy) along which decisions and instructions flow. Span of control is the number of subordinates a manager supervises. (Ref: Nursing Leadership & Management - organisation.)

question_text: Q1. Pulmonary disorders that cause finger-clubbing include:
options: b) Lung cancer, lung abscess, bronchiectasis
c) Cystic fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, pneumothorax
d) Pleural effusion, beryllium disease, chronic atelectasis
answer: Answer: B) Lung cancer, lung abscess, bronchiectasis
rationale: Rationale: Finger-clubbing is associated with chronic suppurative and neoplastic lung disease - classically bronchiectasis, lung abscess, bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer), empyema and pulmonary fibrosis. Asthma, emphysema, pneumonia, pneumothorax and uncomplicated pleural effusion do NOT typically cause clubbing. (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth Medical-Surgical Nursing.)

question_text: Q2. Clinical features of phaeochromocytoma include:
options: a) Muscle weakness, thin skin, raised blood pressure
b) Tingling, muscle spasm, periods of temporary paralysis
c) Excessive facial hair, acne, weight loss
d) Headache, blurring of vision, diaphoresis
answer: Answer: D) Headache, blurring of vision, diaphoresis
rationale: Rationale: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour (usually adrenal medulla) producing the classic triad of severe headache, palpitations and diaphoresis (profuse sweating) together with paroxysmal/sustained hypertension and visual blurring. (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth.)

question_text: Q3. In the management of pemphigus:
options: a) Corticosteroids are administered in high doses until remission is apparent
b) Dapsone is given after screening the patient for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
c) Systemic prednisone is continued for months in alternate-day doses
d) Fluid and electrolyte balance must be maintained to counteract their loss from the skin
answer: Answer: A) Corticosteroids are administered in high doses until remission is apparent
rationale: Rationale: The mainstay of medical management of pemphigus (vulgaris) is high-dose systemic corticosteroids continued until the disease is controlled and the skin is free of blisters (remission), after which the dose is tapered. (Maintaining fluid/electrolyte and protein balance is also an important nursing measure, but the defining first-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids.) (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth - skin disorders.)

question_text: Q4. Surgical management of peptic ulcers is indicated in:
options: a) Severe Helicobacter pylori infection, H2-receptor antagonist resistance
b) Failure to heal after 12-16 weeks of treatment, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
answer: Answer: B) Failure to heal after 12-16 weeks of treatment, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
rationale: Rationale: Surgery for peptic ulcer disease is reserved for intractable disease (failure of adequate medical therapy, e.g. after 12-16 weeks), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and complications (perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage, gastric outlet obstruction). H. pylori, NSAID-induced, stress, Cushing's and Curling's ulcers are managed medically in the first instance. (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth.)

question_text: Q1. The position of choice for a patient who has had a gastrectomy is:
answer: Answer: D) Semi-Fowler's
rationale: Rationale: The semi-Fowler's (semi-sitting) position is used after abdominal surgery such as gastrectomy; it eases respiration and abdominal wall tension, promotes drainage and improves comfort. (Ref: Brunner & Suddarth - post-operative positioning.)
source: [Source paper: April 2025 - NCK BScN Paper 1, April 2025 (candidate recall)]

question_text: Q2. A child is brought after falling down the stairs, complaining of headache and is now unable to move his feet. Using triage colour coding, this client is categorised as:
answer: Answer: D) Red
rationale: Rationale: Inability to move the feet (possible spinal cord injury) following a head injury is a life-/limb-threatening emergency requiring immediate attention - triage RED (immediate). Green = minor, Yellow = urgent but can wait, Black = deceased/expectant. (Ref: MOH Kenya emergency triage - ETAT/MTC.)
source: [Source paper: April 2025 - NCK BScN Paper 1, April 2025 (candidate recall)]

question_text: Q1. The condition for which a nurse prepares a woman for emergency caesarean delivery is:
answer: Answer: A) Prolapsed cord
rationale: Rationale: Cord prolapse is a true obstetric emergency: the presenting part compresses the cord, cutting off fetal oxygen, so an immediate (emergency) caesarean section is indicated if delivery is not imminent. Twin pregnancy, meconium-stained liquor and a non-reactive NST are warning signs that require close monitoring but are not, on their own, automatic indications for emergency caesarean. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives; MOH Kenya Basic Emergency Obstetric & Newborn Care guidelines.)

question_text: Q2. To screen for the presence of neural tube defects in the fetus, the test that would be performed on a pregnant woman is:
answer: Answer: C) Serum alpha-fetoprotein
rationale: Rationale: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) is the standard screening test for open neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida); levels are raised when the defect is open. Amniocentesis is diagnostic/confirmatory (and invasive), the biophysical profile assesses fetal wellbeing, and TORCH titres screen for congenital infection. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives.)

question_text: Q3. During first examination of a normal newborn baby, a nurse would expect to identify:
options: a) Apical pulse rate of 90 beats per minute
b) Hands and feet that have a bluish colour
c) Eye discharge that is yellow and watery
d) Umbilical stump that has two veins and one artery
answer: Answer: B) Hands and feet that have a bluish colour
rationale: Rationale: Acrocyanosis (bluish hands and feet) is a normal finding in the newborn during the first 24-48 hours owing to sluggish peripheral circulation. A normal apical rate is 120-160 b/min (90 is bradycardia); yellow watery eye discharge suggests infection; and a normal cord has TWO arteries and ONE vein (a single artery is abnormal). (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives; MOH Kenya Newborn care.)

question_text: Q4. For a woman who is in labour and experiencing slight shoulder dystocia the nurse would:
options: a) Place her in knee-chest position
b) Apply fundal pressure to the suprapubic area
c) Prepare for assisted forceps delivery
d) Obtain an order for oxytocin infusion
answer: Answer: A) Place her in knee-chest position
rationale: Rationale: The first-line manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia is McRoberts' manoeuvre - sharp hyperflexion of the maternal thighs onto the abdomen (the knee-chest / exaggerated lithotomy position), combined with SUPRAPUBIC (not fundal) pressure. Fundal pressure is contraindicated because it further impacts the shoulder and risks uterine rupture; forceps and oxytocin do not relieve the impacted shoulder. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives; HMS-style obstetric emergency drills.)

question_text: Q5. A labouring woman's husband assists her during the transitional phase of labour. The behaviour that, if exhibited by the husband, would require intervention by a nurse is:
options: a) Offers the woman a bed pan when she needs to have a bowel movement
b) Gives ice-chips to the woman when she says her mouth is dry
c) Provides effleurage when the woman complains of intense abdominal pain
d) Encourages the woman to fix her gaze on him when she experiences a contraction
answer: Answer: A) Offers the woman a bed pan when she needs to have a bowel movement
rationale: Rationale: In the transitional phase an urge to move the bowels usually signals descent of the presenting part and imminent second stage; offering a bedpan could result in delivery onto the pan and is unsafe, so the nurse must intervene/assess for full dilatation. Ice-chips, effleurage and using a focal point are all appropriate, supportive comfort measures. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives.)

question_text: Q6. To help a woman recognise the best time for conceiving, a nurse would instruct the woman to monitor for:
options: a) Drop in body temperature lasting several days
b) Increase in the amount of cervical mucus that is clear and stretchy
c) Abdominal bloating that occurs suddenly
d) Breast tenderness accompanied by slight nipple discharge
answer: Answer: B) Increase in the amount of cervical mucus that is clear and stretchy
rationale: Rationale: Around ovulation, oestrogen causes cervical mucus to become copious, clear, slippery and stretchy (spinnbarkeit) - the most fertile sign. Basal body temperature RISES (does not drop) by about 0.2-0.5C after ovulation; bloating and breast tenderness are non-specific. (Ref: MOH Kenya/WHO Family Planning Guidelines - fertility awareness methods.)

question_text: Q7. The sign that leads a nurse to suspect that a two-week-old infant who was born prematurely may be having apnoea is:
options: a) Intermittent episodes of acrocyanosis for periods of 10 minutes
b) Random episodes of breath-holding during periods of stress
c) Transient episodes of mottling with environmental temperature changes
d) A lapse of spontaneous breathing for 20 seconds
answer: Answer: D) A lapse of spontaneous breathing for 20 seconds
rationale: Rationale: Apnoea of prematurity is defined as cessation of spontaneous breathing for 20 seconds or more, or a shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia/cyanosis/desaturation. Acrocyanosis and mottling with temperature change are normal vasomotor responses. (Ref: MOH Kenya Newborn/Preterm care; Nelson Paediatrics.)

question_text: Q8. When performing a physical assessment of a woman who is 20 weeks pregnant, a nurse would expect to palpate the uterine fundus at:
options: b) Midway between symphysis pubis and umbilicus
d) Midway between umbilicus and xyphoid process
answer: Answer: C) Umbilicus
rationale: Rationale: By approximately 20-22 weeks' gestation the uterine fundus reaches the level of the umbilicus. The fundus is at the symphysis pubis at ~12 weeks, midway between symphysis and umbilicus at ~16 weeks, and near the xiphisternum at ~36 weeks. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - abdominal examination.)

question_text: Q9. A woman complains of morning sickness during the first trimester of pregnancy. To alleviate the symptoms, she should:
options: a) Consume a clear liquid diet
b) Take prenatal vitamins with milk
c) Eat foods that are low in protein
d) Avoid exposure to noxious odours
answer: Answer: D) Avoid exposure to noxious odours
rationale: Rationale: Nausea of early pregnancy is reduced by avoiding triggers such as strong/noxious odours, taking small frequent dry carbohydrate snacks (e.g. dry toast/crackers before rising), and avoiding an empty stomach. A clear-liquid diet is not advised, iron-containing prenatal vitamins often worsen nausea, and protein should NOT be restricted. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - minor disorders of pregnancy.)

question_text: Q10. A primigravida who has had no antenatal care is admitted to the labour ward in active labour. Her cervix is eight centimetres dilated. She starts to push with a contraction. During her next contraction, the nurse should:
options: a) Instruct the patient to take a deep breath, hold it and then bear down
b) Instruct the patient to take short rapid breaths
c) Help the patient to assume a semi-sitting position and hold her knees in a flexed position while bearing down
d) Apply firm pressure on the patient's lower back
answer: Answer: B) Instruct the patient to take short rapid breaths
rationale: Rationale: At 8 cm the cervix is not yet fully dilated, so pushing must be discouraged to avoid cervical oedema and laceration. The woman is taught to pant / take short rapid breaths through the contractions until full dilatation is confirmed. Active bearing-down techniques are appropriate only in the second stage. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives.)

question_text: Q11. The midwife should suspect pregnancy-induced hypertension if, during a client's assessment, she finds the following:
answer: Answer: C) Proteinuria and hypertension
rationale: Rationale: Pre-eclampsia (pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria) is defined by hypertension (BP >=140/90) PLUS proteinuria after 20 weeks. Dependent ankle oedema is common in normal pregnancy, glycosuria suggests gestational diabetes, and pre-eclampsia produces HYPER-reflexia (brisk reflexes/clonus), not hyporeflexia. (Ref: MOH Kenya guidelines on pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; Myles.)

question_text: Q12. The treatment of puerperal mastitis before suppuration occurs is:
options: a) Antibiotics, breast support and ice application
b) Antibiotics, breast support and heat application
c) Antibiotics, aspiration and breast support
d) Antibiotics, incision and drainage, breast support
answer: Answer: B) Antibiotics, breast support and heat application
rationale: Rationale: In the inflammatory (cellulitic) stage of mastitis - before an abscess forms - management is antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal), continued breastfeeding/effective breast emptying, breast support and WARM compresses to promote milk flow and drainage. Incision and drainage (or aspiration) is reserved for an established abscess (suppuration). (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives; MOH Kenya.)

question_text: Q1. The following are clinical types of poliomyelitis: (i) Flaccid poliomyelitis  (ii) Abortive poliomyelitis  (iii) Non-abortive poliomyelitis  (iv) Non-paralytic poliomyelitis
answer: Answer: B) i, ii, iv
rationale: Rationale: The recognised clinical forms of poliomyelitis are abortive (ii), non-paralytic (iv) and paralytic - the latter being flaccid (i). 'Non-abortive' (iii) is not a recognised type and is the distractor, so the correct combination is i, ii, iv. (Ref: Park's/Kenyan Community Health & communicable disease texts; MOH Kenya EPI.)

question_text: Q2. The following are examples of “spacing methods” of family planning:
options: a) Natural methods, chemical barriers, vasectomy
b) Mechanical barriers, tubectomy, chemical barriers
d) Chemical barriers, natural methods, mechanical barriers
answer: Answer: D) Chemical barriers, natural methods, mechanical barriers
rationale: Rationale: Spacing (temporary/reversible) methods allow a couple to delay or space births; they include natural/fertility-awareness methods, chemical barriers (spermicides) and mechanical barriers (condoms, diaphragm). Vasectomy and tubectomy are PERMANENT (terminal) methods, so any option containing them is wrong. (Ref: MOH Kenya National Family Planning Guidelines.)

question_text: Q3. In environmental health, water-based diseases are:
options: a) Due to the presence of an aquatic host
b) Caused by vectors that live near aquatic conditions
c) Caused by poor quality of water
d) Due to inadequate quantities of water
answer: Answer: A) Due to the presence of an aquatic host
rationale: Rationale: Water-based diseases (e.g. schistosomiasis, guinea-worm) require an aquatic intermediate host to complete the parasite's life cycle. This contrasts with water-borne disease (poor water quality, e.g. cholera/typhoid), water-washed disease (inadequate quantity for hygiene) and water-related vector-borne disease (vectors breeding near water, e.g. malaria). (Ref: Kenyan Environmental Health/Community Health texts.)

question_text: Q4. A child with marasmus will present with the following clinical symptoms:
options: a) Oedema of the legs but not the face
answer: Answer: D) No hepatic enlargement
rationale: Rationale: Marasmus is severe wasting from energy deficiency: there is NO oedema, NO hepatomegaly, and NO skin/hair depigmentation - the child is markedly wasted ('old man face') and is usually alert with a relatively good appetite. Oedema, poor appetite, hair/skin depigmentation and a fatty enlarged liver are features of KWASHIORKOR. Hence 'no hepatic enlargement' is correct for marasmus. (Ref: Kenya IMNCI; MOH Kenya/WHO management of acute malnutrition.)

question_text: Q5. In focused antenatal care:
options: a) The mother is encouraged to visit the antenatal clinic at least seven times during pregnancy
b) The mother is encouraged to save some money for buying baby clothes when born
c) The mother is encouraged to decide on the place of birth when labour begins
d) The mother is encouraged to make transport arrangements several months before her time of delivery
answer: Answer: D) The mother is encouraged to make transport arrangements several months before her time of delivery
rationale: Rationale: Focused (goal-directed) antenatal care emphasises birth preparedness and complication readiness - including arranging transport, finances, a skilled birth attendant and place of delivery well in advance. The classic FANC schedule was 4 goal-oriented visits (not seven), and the place of birth is planned during pregnancy, not when labour begins. (Ref: MOH Kenya Focused Antenatal Care guidelines / WHO.)

question_text: Q6. In determination of disease incidence:
options: a) The total population is considered
b) The ability of disease to recur is not considered
c) Persons-years time at risk is considered
d) All the individuals suffering from the disease are considered
answer: Answer: C) Persons-years time at risk is considered
rationale: Rationale: Incidence measures NEW cases arising over time; the incidence rate uses person-time (person-years) at risk as the denominator, counting only those at risk and the time each is observed. Prevalence (not incidence) counts all existing cases. (Ref: Epidemiology - Kenyan Community Health Nursing curriculum.)

question_text: Q7. The demographic trends in Kenya indicate that since 1969 to date:
options: a) The crude birth rate has increased
b) The infant mortality rate has increased
c) Life expectancy at birth has increased
d) Total fertility rate has increased
answer: Answer: C) Life expectancy at birth has increased
rationale: Rationale: Over the decades since 1969, Kenya's life expectancy at birth has risen, while the crude birth rate, infant mortality rate and total fertility rate have all declined (demographic transition). (Ref: KNBS / Kenya Demographic and Health Survey trends.)

question_text: Q8. The following should be highly considered when counselling on family planning for an HIV-positive client:
options: a) Drug interactions between hormonal methods and anti-tuberculosis drugs
b) The client's current stage of AIDS
d) The client's economic status and source of funding
answer: Answer: A) Drug interactions between hormonal methods and anti-tuberculosis drugs
rationale: Rationale: Many HIV-positive clients are on rifampicin-based TB treatment; rifampicin is a potent hepatic enzyme inducer that lowers the blood levels and effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives, so this drug interaction must be considered and an effective/back-up method advised. (Ref: MOH Kenya FP Guidelines; WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria.)

question_text: Q9. When preparing a family for their parents' changed role due to HIV status, an important aspect to consider is:
options: d) Exercise schedule for the infected
answer: Answer: C) De-stigmatisation of the infected
rationale: Rationale: Helping the family understand and accept the diagnosis - reducing stigma and discrimination (de-stigmatisation) toward the infected member - is the priority psychosocial preparation, as stigma undermines disclosure, support, adherence and the family's ability to adapt to changed roles. (Ref: MOH Kenya / NASCOP HIV psychosocial care guidelines.)

question_text: Q10. The resolution stage of the grief response:
options: a) Lasts less than six months
b) May be prolonged if there has been a love-hate association
c) May be prolonged by anticipatory grieving
d) May be of less intensity if the affected has experienced a number of recent losses
answer: Answer: B) May be prolonged if there has been a love-hate association
rationale: Rationale: Resolution of grief is prolonged when the relationship with the deceased was ambivalent (a 'love-hate' association) because of unresolved guilt and conflicting feelings. Anticipatory grieving generally EASES later grief, multiple recent losses tend to INTENSIFY grief, and there is no fixed time limit of under six months. (Ref: Mental Health/Psychiatric Nursing texts.)

question_text: Q11. Mrs. Mama has laid down strict and rigid rules for her baby during toilet training. The characteristics the baby is likely to exhibit in adulthood include: (i) Stubbornness  (ii) Malevolence  (iii) Disorganisation  (iv) Stinginess  (v) Miserliness
answer: Answer: C) i, iv and v
rationale: Rationale: According to Freud's psychosexual theory, conflict/over-strictness during the anal stage (toilet training) produces the 'anal-retentive' personality - obstinacy/stubbornness, orderliness, stinginess and miserliness. Hence i, iv and v. Malevolence and disorganisation are not features (disorganisation is the opposite of the anal-retentive trait). (Ref: Psychiatric/Mental Health Nursing; growth & development.)

question_text: Q12. A patient tells a nurse “I felt very bad when my relatives visited me and I refused to talk to them”. The nurse's best response would be:
options: a) “Did they make you feel that way?”
c) “Do you think they came to visit you just to annoy you?”
d) “Describe what you were feeling just before your relatives visited you”
answer: Answer: D) “Describe what you were feeling just before your relatives visited you”
rationale: Rationale: An open-ended, exploratory statement that invites the patient to describe their feelings ('Describe what you were feeling...') is the therapeutic communication technique of exploring/seeking clarification. The other options are closed, leading or challenging and block communication. (Ref: Therapeutic communication - Mental Health Nursing.)

question_text: Q13. The organic mental syndrome associated with sedative abuse is:
answer: Answer: B) Amnestic syndrome
rationale: Rationale: Chronic sedative (e.g. benzodiazepine/barbiturate) and alcohol abuse classically produces an amnestic syndrome - an inability to form new memories (short-term/recent memory deficit) with relatively preserved attention and remote memory. (Ref: Psychiatric/Mental Health Nursing.)

question_text: Q14. Mini, a 7-year-old boy, has been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The drug group most likely to be used would be:
answer: Answer: D) Central nervous system stimulants
rationale: Rationale: Paradoxically, CNS stimulants (e.g. methylphenidate/Ritalin, dextroamphetamine) are first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD; they increase dopamine/noradrenaline activity and improve attention and impulse control in affected children. (Ref: Pharmacology / Child & Adolescent Mental Health.)

question_text: Q15. Benzhexol (Artane):
options: a) Should not be administered to patients with parkinsonian syndrome
b) May be used safely in patients with prostatic hypertrophy
c) Should never exceed 15 mg daily dosage
d) Does not cause orthostatic hypotension
answer: Answer: C) Should never exceed 15 mg daily dosage
rationale: Rationale: Benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl, Artane) is an anticholinergic used to treat parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal effects; the usual maximum dose is about 15 mg/day. Being anticholinergic it is CONTRAINDICATED in prostatic hypertrophy (risk of urinary retention) - so (A) and (B) are wrong, and it can contribute to orthostatic hypotension. (Ref: Pharmacology texts; BNF.)

question_text: Q16. Exhibitionism:
options: a) Occurs for less than 6 months
b) Occurs equally in both men and women
c) Is intensified when the perpetrator has excess free time and is under significant stress
d) Is more frequent in men without satisfying sexual relationships
answer: Answer: C) Is intensified when the perpetrator has excess free time and is under significant stress
rationale: Rationale: Exhibitionism is a paraphilic disorder (recurrent urges/behaviour of at least 6 months' duration) seen predominantly in men; the urge to expose intensifies when the person has excessive free time or is under significant stress. Many exhibitionists do have satisfying adult sexual relationships, so (D) is incorrect. (Ref: Psychiatric/Mental Health Nursing; DSM criteria.)

question_text: Q17. Children of divorced parents:
options: a) Experience distress and dysfunction more in the year preceding divorce
b) Experience less severe distress after two years of divorce as compared with those children remaining in conflictual marriages
c) Distress and dysfunction are lowest in the year after divorce
d) Have similar psychological problems with those of non-divorced parents
answer: Answer: B) Experience less severe distress after two years of divorce as compared with those children remaining in conflictual marriages
rationale: Rationale: Research shows that, after about two years, children of divorced parents generally adjust and show LESS distress than children who remain in homes with ongoing high parental conflict - i.e., chronic marital conflict is more damaging than the divorce itself once adjustment occurs. (Ref: Child & Family Mental Health.)

question_text: Q18. Mr. Moto has been constantly physically abusing his wife. Mr. Moto:
options: a) Is likely to have a diagnosable mental disorder
b) May predispose his anger on his children
c) May have come from a background in which violence is frequent and tolerated
d) May predispose himself to homicide
answer: Answer: C) May have come from a background in which violence is frequent and tolerated
rationale: Rationale: A learned/socialised history of violence - growing up in a family or environment where violence was frequent and tolerated - is the best-supported correlate of becoming a perpetrator of intimate-partner violence. Most abusers do NOT have a diagnosable mental disorder. (Ref: Mental Health Nursing - family/gender-based violence.)

question_text: Q19. The best management of varicose veins during pregnancy is:
options: a) Using supporting tights or crepe bandage, resting with feet elevated
b) Avoiding standing for too long, wearing loose clothing
c) Avoiding sitting for a long time, elevating feet when sleeping
d) Wearing low-heeled shoes, elevating feet when sleeping
answer: Answer: A) Using supporting tights or crepe bandage, resting with feet elevated
rationale: Rationale: Varicose veins in pregnancy result from impaired venous return; management is supportive - elastic support tights/stockings or a crepe bandage to aid venous return, plus rest with the legs/feet elevated. Avoiding prolonged standing is also advised but the most complete, correct option is A. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - minor disorders of pregnancy.)

question_text: Q20. The management of hypotonic uterine action includes:
options: b) Intravenous infusion of syntocinon in 5% dextrose
c) Intravenous infusion of Buscopan 15 mg
d) Intravenous infusion of syntocinon in normal saline
answer: Answer: D) Intravenous infusion of syntocinon in normal saline
rationale: Rationale: Hypotonic (inefficient) uterine action is corrected by augmenting contractions with an oxytocin (syntocinon) infusion. Current practice dilutes oxytocin in NORMAL SALINE (or Ringer's lactate) rather than dextrose, to avoid hyponatraemia/water intoxication. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives; WHO/MOH Kenya labour management.)

question_text: Q21. When the fetal head is well flexed, the presenting diameters are:
answer: Answer: B) Sub-occipito-bregmatic, biparietal
rationale: Rationale: In a well-flexed vertex presentation the engaging diameters are the sub-occipito-bregmatic (9.5 cm, antero-posterior) and the biparietal (9.5 cm, transverse). The sub-occipito-frontal (10 cm) appears with deflexion, not full flexion. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - fetal skull.)

question_text: Q22. Past obstetric history includes: (i) Any abnormality during previous pregnancies, labour and puerperium  (ii) Age at menarche  (iii) History of twinning in the family  (iv) Miscarriages and gestation when they occurred  (v) Number of children with ages and birth weight
answer: Answer: C) i, iv, v
rationale: Rationale: Past obstetric history covers the woman's PREVIOUS pregnancies - abnormalities of previous pregnancies/labour/puerperium (i), miscarriages and their gestation (iv), and number, ages and birth weights of children (v): i, iv, v. Age at menarche belongs to menstrual history and a family history of twinning to family history. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - history taking.)

question_text: Q23. The muscle layer involved in enmeshing bleeding vessels and preventing bleeding after the delivery of the placenta is:
answer: Answer: B) Middle oblique layer
rationale: Rationale: The middle (oblique) layer of the myometrium has interlacing figure-of-eight fibres surrounding the blood vessels; when it contracts and retracts after the placenta is delivered it compresses the vessels ('living ligatures'), controlling bleeding. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - the uterus.)

question_text: Q24. During the 2nd trimester of pregnancy, the blood pressure falls due to:
options: a) Effects of progesterone on the smooth muscles causing relaxation and dilatation of the arterial wall
b) Effects of oestrogen on the smooth muscles causing relaxation and dilatation of the arterial wall
c) Effects of progesterone on the smooth muscles causing relaxation
d) Effects of oestrogen on the smooth muscles causing relaxation
answer: Answer: A) Effects of progesterone on the smooth muscles causing relaxation and dilatation of the arterial wall
rationale: Rationale: Progesterone relaxes vascular smooth muscle, causing dilatation of the arterial walls and a fall in peripheral resistance; this leads to the mid-pregnancy (2nd-trimester) drop in blood pressure. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - physiological changes in pregnancy.)

question_text: Q25. At the end of pregnancy the total weight gain is expected to be approximately 12 kg, the largest components being:
answer: Answer: D) Fetus and fat
rationale: Rationale: Of the ~12 kg gained in pregnancy, the two largest single components are the fetus (~3.3-3.5 kg) and maternal fat stores (~3.5 kg); the remainder is shared among placenta, amniotic fluid, uterus, breasts, increased blood volume and extracellular fluid. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - weight gain in pregnancy.)

question_text: Q26. The following are positive signs of pregnancy except:
options: a) Visualisation of the fetus by ultrasound
b) Fetal heart sound at 20-24 weeks
c) Presence of human chorionic gonadotrophin in blood or urine (positive pregnancy test)
d) Fetal movement palpable from the 22nd week
answer: Answer: C) Presence of human chorionic gonadotrophin in blood or urine (positive pregnancy test)
rationale: Rationale: Positive (absolute) signs of pregnancy are those that confirm a fetus - ultrasound visualisation, the fetal heart heard by the examiner, and fetal movements palpated by the examiner. A positive hCG pregnancy test is only a PROBABLE sign (it can be positive in molar pregnancy or be falsely positive), so it is the exception. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - diagnosis of pregnancy.)

question_text: Q27. The minor disorders of pregnancy that may progress to major complications include:
options: d) Excessive salivation, nausea and vomiting
answer: Answer: D) Excessive salivation, nausea and vomiting
rationale: Rationale: Nausea and vomiting can progress to hyperemesis gravidarum (with dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and ketosis), and excessive salivation (ptyalism) accompanies and worsens this picture; together they are minor disorders that may become major complications. (Ref: Myles Textbook for Midwives - minor disorders of pregnancy.)

question_text: Q1. Community participation in primary health care (PHC) means the:
options: a) Community must build their health facilities
b) Community assumes responsibility for its health services
c) Leaders of the community should participate in health care
d) Members of the community should engage in health visits
answer: Answer: B) Community assumes responsibility for its health services
rationale: Rationale: A core principle of PHC (Alma-Ata) is community participation - the community is actively involved in planning, implementing and taking responsibility/ownership for its own health and health services, not merely receiving them. (Ref: Community Health Nursing - PHC principles; MOH Kenya.)

question_text: Q2. In descriptive epidemiology the important characteristics of study are:
answer: Answer: A) Demographic data
rationale: Rationale: Descriptive epidemiology characterises the occurrence of disease by PERSON, PLACE and TIME - i.e. demographic data (age, sex, occupation, place, period). Prevalence, incidence and mortality rates are measures of frequency used within (and to support) analytic epidemiology. (Ref: Epidemiology - Kenyan Community Health curriculum.)

question_text: Q3. The group A drugs recommended by WHO for the treatment of gonorrhoea include:
options: c) Amoxycillin 3 g with 1 g of Probenecid orally
answer: Answer: B) I.M Ceftriaxone 250 mg
rationale: Rationale: Ceftriaxone (a third-generation cephalosporin) given as a single intramuscular dose is the WHO/MOH-recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated gonorrhoea (now usually combined with azithromycin owing to resistance). Spectinomycin and others are alternatives/second-line. (Ref: MOH Kenya National STI Management Guidelines; WHO.)

question_text: Q4. To effectively combat endemic malaria, health workers should:
options: a) Distribute insecticide-treated mosquito nets and intensify health education
b) Spray larvicides and cut grass
c) Give more chemoprophylaxis and treat all cases
d) Provide mosquito nets and clear vegetation
answer: Answer: A) Distribute insecticide-treated mosquito nets and intensify health education
rationale: Rationale: Sustainable malaria control combines effective, proven vector control - long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) - with health education to ensure correct, consistent use and prompt treatment-seeking. This integrated, community-based approach is more effective and sustainable than vegetation clearing or blanket chemoprophylaxis. (Ref: MOH Kenya National Malaria Control Programme guidelines.)

question_text: Q5. The immediate treatment for an infant with severe diarrhoea and sunken eyes and fontanelles includes:
options: a) Giving an anti-diarrhoeal drug and admit immediately
b) Taking a blood slide for malarial parasites and then admit
c) Giving intravenous fluids and then admit
d) Giving oral rehydration solution plus an antibiotic
answer: Answer: C) Giving intravenous fluids and then admit
